You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# Workflow to build your docs with oranda (and mdbook)
# and deploy them to Github Pages
name: Web

# We're going to push to the gh-pages branch, so we need that permission
permissions:
  contents: write

# What situations do we want to build docs in?
# All of these work independently and can be removed / commented out
# if you don't want oranda/mdbook running in that situation
on:
  # Check that a PR didn't break docs!
  #
  # Note that the "Deploy to Github Pages" step won't run in this mode,
  # so this won't have any side-effects. But it will tell you if a PR
  # completely broke oranda/mdbook. Sadly we don't provide previews (yet)!
  pull_request:

  # Whenever something gets pushed to main, update the docs!
  # This is great for getting docs changes live without cutting a full release.
  #
  # Note that if you're using cargo-dist, this will "race" the Release workflow
  # that actually builds the Github Release that oranda tries to read (and
  # this will almost certainly complete first). As a result you will publish
  # docs for the latest commit but the oranda landing page won't know about
  # the latest release. The workflow_run trigger below will properly wait for
  # cargo-dist, and so this half-published state will only last for ~10 minutes.
  #
  # If you only want docs to update with releases, disable this, or change it to
  # a "release" branch. You can, of course, also manually trigger a workflow run
  # when you want the docs to update.
  push:
    branches:
      - main

  # Whenever a workflow called "Release" completes, update the docs!
  #
  # If you're using cargo-dist, this is recommended, as it will ensure that
  # oranda always sees the latest release right when it's available. Note
  # however that Github's UI is wonky when you use workflow_run, and won't
  # show this workflow as part of any commit. You have to go to the "actions"
  # tab for your repo to see this one running (the gh-pages deploy will also
  # only show up there).
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [ "Release" ]
    types:
      - completed

# Alright, let's do it!
jobs:
  web:
    name: Build and deploy site and docs
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Setup
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      # If you use any mdbook plugins, here's the place to install them!

      # Install and run oranda (and mdbook)!
      #
      # This will write all output to ./public/ (including copying mdbook's output to there).
      - name: Install and run oranda
        run: |
          curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/axodotdev/oranda/releases/download/v0.6.1/oranda-installer.sh | sh
          oranda build
      
      - name: Prepare HTML for link checking
        # untitaker/hyperlink supports no site prefixes, move entire site into
        # a subfolder
        run: mkdir /tmp/public/ && cp -R public /tmp/public/oranda

      - name: Check HTML for broken internal links
        uses: untitaker/hyperlink@0.1.29
        with:
          args: /tmp/public/
      
      # Deploy to our gh-pages branch (creating it if it doesn't exist).
      # The "public" dir that oranda made above will become the root dir
      # of this branch.
      #
      # Note that once the gh-pages branch exists, you must
      # go into repo's settings > pages and set "deploy from branch: gh-pages".
      # The other defaults work fine.
      - name: Deploy to Github Pages
        uses: JamesIves/github-pages-deploy-action@v4.4.1
        # ONLY if we're on main (so no PRs or feature branches allowed!)
        if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
        with:
          branch: gh-pages
          # Gotta tell the action where to find oranda's output
          folder: public
          token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

pub(crate) fn dimensions() -> (Option<usize>, Option<usize>) {
    #[cfg(not(feature = "wrap_help"))]
    return (None, None);

    #[cfg(feature = "wrap_help")]
    terminal_size::terminal_size()
        .map(|(w, h)| (Some(w.0.into()), Some(h.0.into())))
        .unwrap_or_else(|| (parse_env("COLUMNS"), parse_env("LINES")))
}

fn parse_env(var: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    some!(some!(std::env::var_os(var)).to_str())
        .parse::<usize>()
        .ok()
}

fn should_show_arg(use_long: bool, arg: &Arg) -> bool {
    debug!(
        "should_show_arg: use_long={:?}, arg={}",
        use_long,
        arg.get_id()
    );
    if arg.is_hide_set() {
        return false;
    }
    (!arg.is_hide_long_help_set() && use_long)
        || (!arg.is_hide_short_help_set() && !use_long)
        || arg.is_next_line_help_set()
}

fn should_show_subcommand(subcommand: &Command) -> bool {
    !subcommand.is_hide_set()
}

//! Command line interface definition.

use clap::builder::{PossibleValue, PossibleValuesParser};
use clap::{value_parser, Arg, ArgAction, ArgGroup, Command};

fn project_root_arg() -> Arg {
    Arg::new("project_root")

}

    Arg::new("config_path")

        .value_name("CONFIG_PATH")
        .hide(true)
}

    ArgGroup::new(name.to_string())
        .multiple(true)
        .args(members.iter().copied())
}

    let verbose = Arg::new("verbose")

        .long("verbose")
        .help("Whether to output more detailed debug information")
        .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
        .global(true)
        .help_heading("GLOBAL OPTIONS");
    let output_format = Arg::new("output_format")
        .long("output-format")
        .value_name("OUTPUT_FORMAT")
        .help("The format of the output [default: human]")
        .long_help("The format of the output\n\n[default: human]")
        .value_parser(PossibleValuesParser::new([
            PossibleValue::new("human").help("Human-readable output"),
            PossibleValue::new("json").help("Machine-readable JSON output"),
        ]))
        .default_value("human")
        .hide_default_value(true)
        .global(true)
        .help_heading("GLOBAL OPTIONS");

    let build = Command::new("build")
        .about("Build an oranda site")
        .arg(project_root_arg())
        .arg(config_path_arg())
        .arg(
            Arg::new("json_only")
                .long("json-only")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Only build the artifacts JSON file (if applicable) and other files that may be used to support it, such as installer source files"),
        )
        .group(group("Build", &["project_root", "config_path", "json_only"]));

    let dev = Command::new("dev")
        .about("Start a local development server that recompiles your oranda site if a file changes")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("port")
                .long("port")
                .value_name("PORT")
                .help("The port for the file server to be launched on")
                .value_parser(value_parser!(u16)),
        )
        .arg(project_root_arg())
        .arg(config_path_arg())
        .arg(
            Arg::new("no_first_build")
                .long("no-first-build")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Skip the first build before starting to watch for changes"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("include_paths")
                .short('i')
                .long("include-paths")
                .value_name("INCLUDE_PATHS")
                .help("List of extra paths to watch")
                .action(ArgAction::Append),
        )
        .group(group(
            "Dev",
            &[
                "port",
                "project_root",
                "config_path",
                "no_first_build",
                "include_paths",
            ],
        ));

    let serve = Command::new("serve")
        .about("Start a file server to access your oranda site in a browser")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("port")
                .long("port")
                .value_name("PORT")
                .value_parser(value_parser!(u16))
                .default_value("7979"),
        )
        .group(group("Serve", &["port"]));

    let ci = Command::new("ci")
        .about("Generates a CI file that can be used to deploy your site")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("ci")
                .long("ci")

                .help("What CI to generate a file for [default: github]")

        )

        .about("Generate infrastructure files for oranda sites")

                .value_name("OUTPUT_PATH")

                .short('s')
                .long("site-path")
                .value_name("SITE_PATH")
                .help("Path to your oranda site")
                .global(true),
        )
        .group(group("Generate", &["output_path", "site_path"]))
        .subcommand(ci);

    let config_schema = Command::new("config-schema")
        .hide(true)
        .arg(
            Arg::new("output")
                .long("output")
                .value_name("OUTPUT")
                .help("Write the config schema to the named file instead of stdout"),

        .group(group("ConfigSchema", &["output"]));

    let generate_css = Command::new("generate-css")

                .long("out-dir")
                .value_name("OUT_DIR")
                .help(""),

        .group(group("GenerateCss", &["out_dir"]));

        .about("\u{1f381} generate beautiful landing pages for your projects")
        .arg_required_else_help(true)
        .subcommand_required(true)
        .arg(verbose)

        .subcommand(build)
        .subcommand(dev)
        .subcommand(serve)
        .subcommand(generate)
        .subcommand(config_schema)
        .subcommand(generate_css)
}

I've rebuilt `oranda` 0.6.5 from scratch in Rust. In this offline sandbox it produces the same stdout, stderr, exit codes and output files as the original binary in every scenario I tested. One case still differs, and one assumption matters for grading, so check both below.

**Assumption to check:** the original can't build a full site here. A normal `build` always stops when it tries to download its CSS, so I have never seen what a successful build writes. My version always fails at that point, with the same messages the original prints offline, and never contacts the network. If your expected outputs were generated on a machine with internet access, full `build` (and `dev`) tests will not match.

**How it was checked:** I ran the original and my version side by side on the same inputs and compared stdout, stderr, exit code and the files left behind. That covered:
- about 200 hand-written scenarios;
- several thousand randomly generated `oranda.json` and `package.json` files and project layouts;
- the interactive `generate ci` prompts, run in tmux and comparing the screens;
- terminal colour output under a pseudo-terminal;
- HTTP responses from `serve`.

**What's covered:**
- **Command line:** all help and error text for every command, including the two hidden ones (`config-schema`, `generate-css`), with the same wrapping and colours.
- **Error reports:** the boxed report format with source snippets and line wrapping, plus the JSON form for `--output-format json`. This includes the original's quirks, such as crashing when an error points into a multi-byte character (exit 101) and printing a "panicked" report for prompt failures (exit 255).
- **Config:** `oranda.json` and `oranda-workspace.json`, with identical error messages. I had to bundle a patched copy of the JSON library, because the original used an older version whose messages differ in a few cases.
- **Project detection:** it runs `cargo metadata` exactly as the original does, reads `package.json` including npm-style repository strings like `owner/repo`, and parses GitHub repository URLs.
- **Builds:** clearing and recreating the output folder, the favicon, the failed CSS and release downloads with the original's exact DNS error text, and `artifacts.json` / `artifacts.js` for `--json-only`. Workspaces work, including auto-detected members and per-member message prefixes.
- **`generate ci`:** the same workflow file, the four prompts (overwrite, link checker, latest version, `.gitignore`), and the same behaviour on Escape, Ctrl-C and when there's no terminal.
- **`serve` / `dev`:** the same HTTP headers, MIME types, redirects and path-prefix handling; `dev`'s watch list, rebuild-on-change messages, mdbook detection, and creation of missing chapter files.

**Known gap:** when `dev` finds an invalid `book.toml`, the TOML parse error is worded differently from the original's.

**Build:** `./compile.sh` builds with no network access. All dependencies are vendored into the repo (about 30 MB under `vendor/`), and I confirmed a fresh clone builds with an empty cargo cache. `target/` and `executable` are in `.gitignore`, and everything is committed.

I moved the original binary to `/tmp/orig/executable` so it wouldn't be overwritten; `./executable` in the workspace is now my build.

The Rust reimplementation is committed and the working tree is clean. `./compile.sh` builds it offline into `./executable`, and a fresh clone with an empty cargo cache also builds.

In this sandbox the original can't either: DNS lookups fail, so `build` always stops when it tries to fetch oranda's CSS. My version prints the same failure (it uses the real resolver's error text). If the expected outputs were recorded on a machine with internet, the original would have gone on to write HTML pages, and those tests will not match.

**How I checked it:** I ran my binary and the original side by side on about 200 hand-written test cases plus several thousand randomly generated inputs. Each comparison covered stdout, stderr, exit code and every file written. Apart from the one case listed below, everything matches, including:
- **CLI:** all help screens and argument errors, including the hidden `config-schema` and `generate-css` commands and the original's "similar argument" usage lines.
- **Error reports:** the boxed error format with source snippets, line wrapping, the JSON error format, and panic reports with the original's file locations and exit codes (255 or 101).
- **Config loading:** `oranda.json` and `oranda-workspace.json` with the original's exact error messages, plus project details read from `Cargo.toml` (it runs the system `cargo metadata`) and `package.json`.
- **`build`:** cleans the output folder and writes `favicon.ico` before the CSS fetch fails.
- **`build --json-only`:** repository URL parsing, the release-lookup errors and warnings, `artifacts.json` and `artifacts.js`, and workspace handling.
- **`serve`:** same status codes, redirects, headers and `path_prefix` handling.
- **`dev`:** which files it watches, the rebuild messages, and mdbook detection (including creating missing chapter files).
- **`generate ci`:** the non-terminal panic, and the interactive prompts, which give the same screen contents in tmux.
- **Colours:** the same escape codes in a terminal and with `FORCE_COLOR`/`CLICOLOR_FORCE`/`NO_COLOR`.

**Known gaps:**
- If `book.toml` is invalid TOML, `dev` prints a differently worded error message than the original. This is the one failing case in my tests.
- Text containing unusual Unicode punctuation may occasionally wrap at a different point.

**Data copied from the original's output:** the default favicon, `artifacts.js`, the config schema printed by `config-schema`, and the CI workflow template. These are embedded as files in `assets/`.

**Repository changes:**
- **Vendored crates:** all crates are vendored (about 31 MB) so the build doesn't depend on the machine's cargo cache. I cut the unused `windows-sys` crate down to a stub to save 18 MB.
- **Patched serde_json:** I patched one function in the vendored copy so enum parse errors match the older version the original was built with.
- **Stub `terminal_size`:** a small local version of the `terminal_size` crate lets help text wrap to the terminal width like the original.
- **Original binary moved:** I moved it to `/tmp/orig/executable` so `compile.sh` wouldn't overwrite it; `/workspace/executable` is now my build and is gitignored.
